title_ar: حكم الصلاة في مسجد أقيم في مكان غير مشرع من طرف الدولة
title_en: The ruling on praying in a mosque built on land not authorised by the state
body_ar:
بعض الأئمة في الجمعة الماضية يقول بأن الصلاة في هذا المسجد ليست صحيحة وذلك لأنه مكزور؟

أن المساجد لا تدخل في حيز ما يسمى بالكزرة، قد ذكرنا أن الكزرة هي الإحياء بالقسر أي التملك بقسر من غير إذن، والمساجد ملك عام للناس فليست ملكا شخصيا ومن هنا فلا تدخل في ذلك فهي لله سبحانه وتعالى حررها من ملك العباد ومن ملك الأغيار فلا تدخل في هذا القبيل أصلا.
body_en:
One of the imams said last Friday that prayer in this mosque is not valid, because it is makzūr [built on land taken without authorisation]?

Mosques do not fall within the scope of what is called al-kazrah. We have already said that al-kazrah is bringing land into use by force — that is, taking ownership by force, without permission. Mosques are the common property of the people, not anyone's personal property, and for that reason they do not come under this. They belong to God, glorified and exalted, who has freed them from the ownership of His servants and from the ownership of others, so they do not fall into this category at all.

flags.context: بعض الأئمة ... يقول بأن الصلاة في هذا المسجد ليست صحيحة وذلك لأنه مكزور؟ ... أن الكزرة هي الإحياء بالقسر أي التملك بقسر من غير إذن
options: appropriation of land by force without permit (al-kazrah)
flags.note: Mauritanian (Hassaniya) regional term with no settled English equivalent; it does not appear in the classical fiqh lexicon. The Sheikh supplies his own definition in the text — iḥyāʾ (bringing dead land into productive use, the classical doctrine of iḥyāʾ al-mawāt) carried out coercively and without permission — so the definition, not the label, carries the meaning. The Arabic label is kept in brackets throughout. The Sheikh's office should confirm whether kazrah in current Mauritanian usage means specifically occupation of state land without a permit, which is what the article's title implies, or any forcible appropriation.

translator_notes: Qur'anic and hadith renderings in this file are interpretive translations of meaning, offered to carry the Sheikh's argument in English. They are not a substitute for the Arabic.

In the source, the answer begins with the elliptical particle 'anna ('[the answer is] that ...'), the Joomla fatwa template's standing form. The English drops the particle and begins the sentence directly; no content is added or removed by this.

The date shown by the CMS (27 December 2010) is a bulk-upload timestamp shared by every item in this range, not the date the Sheikh gave the answer. The real date of composition is unknown. See date_is_cms_bulk_upload.
'Not valid' renders 'laysat ṣaḥīḥah', which concerns the validity of the prayer, not its sinfulness. The questioner's claim is that the prayer does not count, not merely that it is blameworthy.
The Sheikh answers that mosques are not subject to the doctrine at all. He does not go on to state in so many words that the prayer is therefore valid, and the English does not supply that step.
